{{Short description|Concept in mathematics}}
[[File:Parabolic cylindrical coordinates.png|thumb|right|350px|[[Coordinate system#Coordinate surface|Coordinate surfaces]] of parabolic cylindrical coordinates. Parabolic cylinder functions occur when [[separation of variables]] is used on [[Laplace's equation]] in these coordinates]]
[[File:Plot of the parabolic cylinder function D v(z) with v=5 in the complex plane from -2-2i to 2+2i with colors created with Mathematica 13.1 function ComplexPlot3D.svg|alt=Plot of the parabolic cylinder function ''D''<sub>''ν''</sub>(''z'') with ''ν'' = 5 in the complex plane from -2-2i to 2+2i|thumb|Plot of the parabolic cylinder function ''D''<sub>''ν''</sub>(''z'') with {{nowrap|1=''ν'' = 5}} in the complex plane from {{nowrap|−2 − 2''i''}} to {{nowrap|2 + 2''i''}}]]
In [[mathematics]], the '''parabolic cylinder functions''' are [[special functions]] defined as solutions to the differential equation

{{NumBlk|:|<math>\frac{d^2f}{dz^2} + \left(\tilde{a}z^2+\tilde{b}z+\tilde{c}\right)f=0.</math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}

This equation is found when the technique of [[separation of variables]] is used on [[Laplace's equation]] when expressed in [[parabolic cylindrical coordinates]].

The above equation may be brought into two distinct forms (A) and (B) by  [[completing the square]] and rescaling {{mvar|z}}, called [[H. F. Weber]]'s equations:<ref name="Weber"/>
{{NumBlk|:|<math>\frac{d^2f}{dz^2} - \left(\tfrac14z^2+a\right)f=0</math>|{{EquationRef|A}}}}
and
{{NumBlk|:|<math>\frac{d^2f}{dz^2} + \left(\tfrac14z^2-a\right)f=0.</math>|{{EquationRef|B}}}}

If <math display="block">f(a,z)</math> is a solution, then so are
<math display="block">f(a,-z), f(-a,iz)\text{ and  }f(-a,-iz).</math>

If <math display="block">f(a,z)\,</math> is a solution of equation ({{EquationNote|A}}), then <math display="block">f(-ia,ze^{(1/4)\pi i})</math> is a solution of ({{EquationNote|B}}), and, by symmetry,
<math display="block">f(-ia,-ze^{(1/4)\pi i}), f(ia,-ze^{-(1/4)\pi i})\text{ and }f(ia,ze^{-(1/4)\pi i})</math>
are also solutions of ({{EquationNote|B}}).

== Solutions ==

There are independent even and odd solutions of the form ({{EquationNote|A}}). These are given by (following the notation of [[Abramowitz and Stegun]] (1965)):<ref name="Abramowitz-Stegun"/>
<math display="block">y_1(a;z) = \exp(-z^2/4) \;_1F_1 
\left(\tfrac12a+\tfrac14; \;
\tfrac12\; ; \; \frac{z^2}{2}\right)\,\,\,\,\,\, (\mathrm{even})</math>
and 
<math display="block">y_2(a;z) = z\exp(-z^2/4) \;_1F_1 
\left(\tfrac12a+\tfrac34; \;
\tfrac32\; ; \; \frac{z^2}{2}\right)\,\,\,\,\,\, (\mathrm{odd})</math>
where <math>\;_1F_1 (a;b;z)=M(a;b;z)</math> is the [[confluent hypergeometric function]].

Other pairs of independent solutions may be formed from linear combinations of the above solutions.<ref name="Abramowitz-Stegun"/> One such pair is based upon their behavior at infinity:
<math display="block">
U(a,z)=\frac{1}{2^\xi\sqrt{\pi}}
\left[
\cos(\xi\pi)\Gamma(1/2-\xi)\,y_1(a,z)
-\sqrt{2}\sin(\xi\pi)\Gamma(1-\xi)\,y_2(a,z)
\right]
</math>
<math display="block">
V(a,z)=\frac{1}{2^\xi\sqrt{\pi}\Gamma[1/2-a]}
\left[
\sin(\xi\pi)\Gamma(1/2-\xi)\,y_1(a,z)
+\sqrt{2}\cos(\xi\pi)\Gamma(1-\xi)\,y_2(a,z)
\right]
</math>
where <math display="block"> \xi = \frac{1}{2}a+\frac{1}{4} .</math>

The function {{math|''U''(''a'', ''z'')}} approaches zero for large values of {{mvar|z}} and {{math|{{!}}arg(''z''){{!}} < ''π''/2}}, while {{math|''V''(''a'', ''z'')}} diverges for large values of positive real {{mvar|z}}.
<math display="block"> \lim_{z\to\infty}U(a,z)/\left(e^{-z^2/4}z^{-a-1/2}\right)=1\,\,\,\,(\text{for}\,\left|\arg(z)\right|<\pi/2) </math>
and
<math display="block"> \lim_{z\to\infty}V(a,z)/\left(\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}e^{z^2/4}z^{a-1/2}\right)=1\,\,\,\,(\text{for}\,\arg(z)=0) . </math>

For [[half-integer]] values of ''a'', these (that is, ''U'' and ''V'') can be re-expressed in terms of [[Hermite polynomials]]; alternatively, they can also be expressed in terms of [[Bessel function]]s.

The functions ''U'' and ''V'' can also be related to the functions {{math|1=''D<sub>p</sub>''(''x'')}} (a notation dating back to Whittaker (1902))<ref name="Whittaker"/> that are themselves sometimes called parabolic cylinder functions:<ref name="Abramowitz-Stegun"/>
<math display="block">\begin{align}
U(a,x) &= D_{-a-\tfrac12}(x), \\
V(a,x) &= \frac{\Gamma(\tfrac12+a)}{\pi}[\sin( \pi a) D_{-a-\tfrac12}(x)+D_{-a-\tfrac12}(-x)] .
\end{align}</math>

Function {{math|1=''D<sub>a</sub>''(''z'')}} was introduced by Whittaker and Watson as a solution of eq.~({{EquationNote|1}}) with <math display="inline">\tilde a=-\frac14, \tilde b=0, \tilde c=a+\frac12</math> bounded at <math>+\infty</math>.<ref name="Whittaker-Watson"/> It can be expressed in terms of confluent hypergeometric functions as
:<math>D_a(z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi }}{2^{a/2} e^{-\frac{z^2}{4}} \left(\cos \left(\frac{\pi  a}{2}\right) \Gamma \left(\frac{a+1}{2}\right) \, _1F_1\left(-\frac{a}{2};\frac{1}{2};\frac{z^2}{2}\right)+\sqrt{2} z \sin \left(\frac{\pi  a}{2}\right) \Gamma \left(\frac{a}{2}+1\right) \, _1F_1\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{a}{2};\frac{3}{2};\frac{z^2}{2}\right)\right)}.</math>
[[Power series]] for this function have been obtained by Abadir (1993).<ref name="Abadir"/>

== Parabolic Cylinder U(a,z) function ==
=== Integral representation ===
Integrals along the [[Number line|real line]],<ref name="DLMF"/>
<math display="block">
U(a,z)=\frac{e^{-\frac14 z^2}}{\Gamma\left(a+\frac12\right)}
\int_0^\infty e^{-zt}t^{a-\frac12}e^{-\frac12 t^2}dt
\,,\; \Re a>-\frac12 \;,
</math>
<math display="block">
U(a,z)=\sqrt{\frac2{\pi}}e^{\frac14 z^2}
\int_0^\infty \cos\left(zt+\frac{\pi}{2}a+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
t^{-a-\frac12}e^{-\frac12 t^2}dt
\,,\; \Re a<\frac12 \;.
</math>
The fact that these integrals are solutions to equation&nbsp;({{EquationNote|A}}) can be easily checked by direct substitution.

=== Derivative ===
Differentiating the integrals with respect to <math>z</math> gives two expressions for <math>U'(a,z)</math>,
<math display="block">
U'(a,z)=-\frac{z}{2}U(a,z)-
\frac{e^{-\frac14 z^2}}{\Gamma\left(a+\frac12\right)}
\int_0^\infty e^{-zt}t^{a+\frac12}e^{-\frac12 t^2}dt
=-\frac{z}{2}U(a,z)-\left(a+\frac12\right)U(a+1,z) \;,
</math>
<math display="block">
U'(a,z)=\frac{z}{2}U(a,z)-
\sqrt{\frac2{\pi}}e^{\frac14 z^2}
\int_0^\infty \sin\left(zt+\frac{\pi}{2}a+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
t^{-a+\frac12}e^{-\frac12 t^2}dt
= \frac{z}{2}U(a,z)-U(a-1,z) \;.
</math>
Adding the two gives another expression for the derivative,
<math display="block">
2U'(a,z) = -\left(a+\frac12\right)U(a+1,z)-U(a-1,z)
\;.
</math>

=== Recurrence relation ===
Subtracting the first two expressions for the derivative gives the recurrence relation,
<math display="block">
zU(a,z) = U(a-1,z) - \left(a+\frac12\right)U(a+1,z) \;.
</math>

=== Asymptotic expansion ===
Expanding
<math display="block">
e^{-\frac12 t^2}=1-\frac12 t^2+\frac18 t^4 - \dots \;
</math>
in the integrand of the integral representation
gives the asymptotic expansion of <math>U(a,z)</math>,
<math display="block">
U(a,z) = e^{-\frac14 z^2}z^{-a-\frac12}\left(1
- \frac{(a+\frac12)(a+\frac32)}{2}\frac{1}{z^2}
+ \frac{(a+\frac12)(a+\frac32)(a+\frac52)(a+\frac72)}{8}\frac{1}{z^4}
- \dots\right) .
</math>

=== Power series ===
Expanding the integral representation in powers of <math>z</math> gives
<math display="block">
U(a,z)=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}\,2^{-\frac{a}{2}-\frac14}}{\Gamma\left(\frac{a}{2}+\frac34\right)}
-\frac{\sqrt{\pi}\,2^{-\frac{a}{2}+\frac14}}{\Gamma\left(\frac{a}{2}+\frac14\right)}z
+\frac{\sqrt{\pi}\,2^{-\frac{a}{2}-\frac54}}{\Gamma\left(\frac{a}{2}+\frac34\right)}z^2 - \dots \;.
</math>

=== Values at z=0 ===
From the power series one immediately gets
<math display="block">
U(a,0)=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}\,2^{-\frac{a}{2}-\frac14}}{\Gamma\left(\frac{a}{2}+\frac34\right)} \;,
</math>
<math display="block">
U'(a,0)=-\frac{\sqrt{\pi}\,2^{-\frac{a}{2}+\frac14}}{\Gamma\left(\frac{a}{2}+\frac14\right)} \;.
</math>

== Parabolic cylinder D<sub>&nu;</sub>(z) function ==
Parabolic cylinder function <math>D_\nu(z)</math> is the solution to the Weber [[differential equation]],
<math display="block">
u''+\left(\nu+\frac12-\frac{1}{4} z^2 \right)u=0 \,,
</math>
that is regular at <math>\Re z\to +\infty</math> with the asymptotics
<math display="block">
D_\nu(z) \to e^{-\frac14 z^2}z^\nu \,.
</math>
It is thus given as <math>D_\nu(z)=U(-\nu-1/2,z)</math> and its properties then directly follow from those of the <math>U</math>-function.
=== Integral representation ===
<math display="block">
D_\nu(z)=\frac{e^{-\frac14 z^2}}{\Gamma(-\nu)}
\int_0^\infty e^{-zt} t^{-\nu -1} e^{-\frac12 t^2}dt
\,,\; \Re \nu < 0 \,,\; \Re z > 0\;,
</math>
<math display="block">
D_\nu(z)=\sqrt{\frac2{\pi}}e^{\frac14 z^2}
\int_0^\infty \cos\left(zt-\nu \frac{\pi}{2}\right)
t^{\nu}e^{-\frac12 t^2}dt
\,,\; \Re \nu > -1 \;.
</math>

=== Asymptotic expansion ===
<math display="block">
D_\nu(z) = e^{-\frac14 z^2}z^{\nu}\left(1
- \frac{\nu (\nu -1)}{2}\frac{1}{z^2}
+ \frac{\nu (\nu -1)(\nu -2)(\nu -3)}{8}\frac{1}{z^4}
- \dots\right)\,,\; \Re z \to +\infty .
</math>
If <math>\nu</math> is a non-negative integer this series terminates and turns into a polynomial, namely the [[Hermite polynomial]],
<math display="block">
D_n(z) = e^{-\frac14 z^2}\;2^{-n/2}H_n\left(\frac{z}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\,, n=0,1,2,\dots \;.
</math>

=== Connection with quantum harmonic oscillator ===
Parabolic cylinder <math>D_\nu(z)</math> function appears naturally in the [[Schrödinger equation]] for the one-dimensional [[quantum harmonic oscillator]] (a quantum particle in the oscillator potential),
<math display="block">
\left[-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}+\frac12 m \omega^2 x^2 \right]\psi(x)
=E\psi(x) \;,
</math>
where
<math>\hbar</math> is the reduced [[Planck constant]],
<math>m</math> is the mass of the particle,
<math>x</math> is the coordinate of the particle,
<math>\omega</math> is the frequency of the oscillator,
<math>E</math> is the energy,
and <math>\psi(x)</math> is the particle's wave-function. Indeed introducing the new quantities
<math display="block">
z=\frac{x}{b_o} \,,\; \nu=\frac{E}{\hbar\omega}-\frac12 \,,\; b_o=\sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2m\omega}} \,,
</math>
turns the above equation into the Weber's equation for the function <math>u(z)=\psi(zb_o)</math>,
<math display="block">
u''+\left(\nu+\frac12-\frac{1}{4} z^2 \right)u=0 \,.
</math>
